transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-07
Start time: 06:30 JST
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (SE), Sasha Ortiz (Product) -- Aiko Tanaka, Kenji Sato, Priya Nair, Dinesh Rao (KumoHealth)

Summary:
Short hosted generative demo oriented to APAC latency concerns, region pinning, basic streaming parameters, retry semantics and quick cost controls in the Console/Optimize. Agreed next steps include sandbox invite, latency run, and pricing sheet for dedicated pool POC.

Topics:
- APAC region latency + dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
- Streaming behavior and client retry patterns
- Pinning model versions and fallback policies
- Console Optimize suggestions (batching, quantization recommendations)
- Security/compliance ask: SOC2, VPC/private plane questions

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Alright hi everybody, thanks for making the time early this morning. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Uh, quick intros — Ravi from SE, Sasha from product.
[00:07] Maya: Aiko, Kenji, Priya, Dinesh -- do you want to intro quickly?
[00:11] Aiko: Yeah sure, I'm Aiko, lead engineer on the conv platform at KumoHealth. We're building patient-facing chat and triage flows.
[00:18] Kenji: Kenji, platform PM. We'll be owning the integration and infra pieces.
[00:22] Priya: Priya, CTO, I'll be involved on the SRE/compliance side.
[00:26] Dinesh: Dinesh SRE. I'll run the tests with you.
[00:29] Maya: Great — plan for today, short hosted demo of chat gen streaming, show parameter tuning in Console, then Ravi will go into retry/fallback patterns, and we'll leave time for Q+A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:39] Aiko: Sounds good. We mostly want to understand latency for ap-northeast-1 and the failover behaviours. Also cost ballpark.
[00:45] Maya: Perfect. I'll share my screen — bear with me while I pull up the demo org.
[00:52] (screen share noise)
[01:05] Maya: Okay, so I'm in the Redwood Console. First thing: the API key and region selection. For APAC we have ap-northeast-1 and ap-southeast-1 regions — hosted endpoints close to your clusters.
[01:20] Aiko: Quick question: is data ever routed out of-region for model inference?
[01:24] Ravi: Good question — for hosted API when you choose a region, inference occurs in that region; fallback will only go cross-region if you configure multi-region fallback policy. By default we keep requests in-region, though logs/audit events might be stored in the control plane region unless you enable private deployment.
[01:39] Kenji: So for latency sensitive flows we should pin to ap-northeast-1, correct?
[01:43] Ravi: Yes pinning model version + region is the typical approach. You can pin in the route config, and then configure an automatic fallback to a compatible quantized or smaller variant if capacity is constrained.
[01:55] Maya: I'll open a quick trace — here's a live chat request hitting the hosted endpoint, streaming back tokens.
[02:03] (typing)
[02:07] [02:07] Maya: Sending a 350-token prompt simulating a triage question. You'll see the stream chunking every ~200ms; that's the runtime's continuous-batching emitter.
[02:16] [02:16] Maya: -- and we get the partial tokens. You might notice the punctuation sometimes comes in later, that's normal for streaming.
[02:23] Aiko: Right, how should our client do retries if a partial stream fails?
[02:27] Ravi: We generally recommend idempotent request keys on the client and short exponential backoff—so the client can request a retry for the same request id and the server will attempt to resume from last committed KV offset if supported.
[02:38] Priya: KV offset? can you explain that?
[02:41] Ravi: Sure — the runtime maintains a KV cache for token keys to speed up autoregressive decoding. On the protocol side, we expose a continuation token for some model variants that lets the server continue generation without recomputing prefixes. Not all community models support that, but many optimized variants in our catalog do.
[02:58] Dinesh: I think our client library is in Go and we want to avoid duplicate completions. So the idempotency approach plus checking the streamed 'final' flag makes sense.
[03:07] Maya: Exactly — one common pattern we demo: on reconnect, attempt to use the server-side resume token; if not present then perform a fresh request with same id and let the server dedupe via request metadata.
[03:19] Kenji: And what about the 99th percentile? we need hard numbers for SLA discussions.
[03:24] Ravi: We typically provide region-specific 50/95/99 numbers for model families. I'll run a quick benchmark with your sample prompts — tho I'll need your traffic profile and token length distribution to match.
[03:36] Sasha: Also worth noting: our Optimize tab will suggest batching and quantization to hit cost targets. If you upload a small sample workload it will make model/quantization recommendations and simulated cost savings.
[03:49] Aiko: That sounds neat. Can you show the Optimize flow?
[03:51] Maya: Yep, switching tabs to Optimize — here's a small workload I uploaded earlier. You can see the suggestion: for your mostly short-turn triage questions, we recommend the small-8q variant which reduces token compute by ~4x with a small quality delta.
[04:06] Priya: What's the quality delta? we can't afford hallucinations on medical guidance.
[04:10] Sasha: Good callout. Optimize shows a precision metric on your eval set; for this sample it estimates <0.5% drop in label accuracy for our eval prompts. But for production we recommend a guardrail eval with your clinical prompts — we don't push quantized models into clinical prod without you validating.
[04:27] Kenji: Ok, how do rollouts work? can we canary to 5% traffic and then increase?
[04:31] Maya: Yep, the rollout UI supports canary percentages, weighted routing per model version, and automatic health-based rollbacks. You can also configure a fallback policy to a different model family in case of QoS regressions.
[04:44] Aiko: On the security side — we need SOC2, SSO, and the option for a VPC/private control plane.
[04:50] Maya: Short answer: SOC2 Type II yes, SSO via SAML/SCIM is supported, and we offer Redwood Private with a customer-controlled control plane or fully on-prem package for air-gapped needs. I'll share the security deck after the call.
[05:03] Priya: Do logs show full request payloads? we need to ensure PHI is handled correctly.
[05:08] Ravi: For hosted by default we store transcripts in the control plane for 30 days; however you can opt-out of storage or use Dedicated/Private where we can flush or route logs to your KMS-backed storage. We also support token redaction in traces if you want to prevent full PHI being stored.
[05:24] Dinesh: Great — KMS integration, is that AWS KMS or do you support HSM?
[05:29] Sasha: We integrate with AWS KMS and Azure Key Vault, and enterprise customers can bring their own HSM for Private deployments.
[05:36] Maya: Okay, now I'll do a quick live failover demo — I'll intentionally block ap-northeast-1 for a route to simulate capacity fail and show fallback to ap-southeast-1 and a smaller quantized variant.
[05:46] (pause, typing)
[06:01] Maya: Sending requests; you'll see longer tail while we re-route then the client shows resumed stream. Note the minor latency increase due to cross-region hop.
[06:11] Aiko: So for a global product we probably want primary in APAC and fall back to asia-southeast only in emergencies, yes?
[06:16] Ravi: Exactly. You can tailor failures by policy: prefer local region, but fail over to nearest region and then to a cheaper capacity tier.
[06:26] Kenji: Can we set hard limits to avoid cross-region cost surprises?
[06:30] Maya: Yep, in the route config you can set cost caps and prevent cross-region fallback — the request would then receive a capacity_error instead of failing over.
[06:39] Priya: Back to retries — what does an ideal client library integration look like for streaming in JS/Go?
[06:46] Ravi: For streaming: open stream with idempotent request id, listen for partial chunks with timestamps, if stream disconnects then attempt resume using the continuation token; if resume token not available, do fresh request with same id and rely on server dedupe. For backoff we recommend jittered exponential with max ~8s.
[07:08] Aiko: What's the recommended token size for prompts to keep latency below 200ms p50?
[07:12] Ravi: CPU/GPU characteristics and model choice matter; for our smaller chat-optimized variants you can expect p50 under 120ms for 32-64 token prompts; 350 token prompts push p50 higher and definitely increase p95/p99. For triage we see a lot of shorter prompts which is good for latency.
[07:30] Dinesh: Are there per-request options to prioritize latency over cost?
[07:34] Maya: Yes, you can set a priority flag in the API route to prefer low-latency pools (higher cost). The Console has a per-route override for priority tiers.
[07:43] Kenji: Could you show a sample of the API request and streaming response?
[07:47] Maya: Sure, here's a curl sample and then the JS streaming snippet. (reads) POST /v1/chat with headers: Authorization, X-Region, Idempotency-Key. Body: {model: "redwood-chat-small", messages: [...], stream: true}. Response chunks look like {delta: "...", final: false, token_index: 234}.
[08:10] Aiko: I noticed in previous calls some of the model names are different — how does the catalog naming map to familiar family names?
[08:15] Sasha: We provide a catalog mapping and performance profiles. Each model entry shows token throughput, recommended batch sizes, and supported runtime features (resume tokens, kv-cache).
[08:26] Priya: On billing — is it per-token only? or are there overheads?
[08:30] Maya: Hosted API is per-token with tiered pricing; Dedicated adds a base reserved capacity fee plus reduced per-token compute. We also have egress/network pass-through invoicing if Private setups require dedicated peering.
[08:45] Kenji: For a POC with expected 500 reqs/min at 60 tokens avg, what would you recommend?
[08:51] Ravi: For that scale, a small Dedicated pool or high-tier hosted plan will be most predictable. I'll run numbers and include a worksheet in the quote.
[08:59] Aiko: Can we demo the Console's usage breakdown?
[09:02] Maya: Sure — switching to the Console usage tab. Here you can filter by token type, model, and route. Cost heatmaps show token-weighted spend per route per day.
[09:15] Dinesh: Is it possible to have token-level alerts for sudden spikes?
[09:18] Sasha: Yes, set alerts on per-route token volume, 95th percentile latency, or error spike — those trigger webhooks and pager integrations.
[09:27] Kenji: Any gotchas when using streaming + websockets vs server-sent events?
[09:32] Ravi: Websockets give you full-duplex and lower overhead for many small messages; SSE is simpler for one-directional streams. Both supported. For mobile, we often recommend SSE for simplicity unless you need client-to-server intermediate messages.
[09:47] Aiko: Ok, we've covered most dev patterns — one last question on retention: for compliance we need 7 years of audit logs. Is that an option?
[09:55] Maya: For enterprise Private deployments we can support longer retention, export to your S3 with lifecycle policies. Hosted has configurable retention windows but not typically 7 years unless we do a custom enterprise agreement.
[10:09] Priya: Understood — we'll check requirements and flag if 7-years is non-negotiable.
[10:14] Maya: Great. Ravi, I'm going to hand over to you for a short technical deep dive on retry edge cases and a couple of live failure mode tests.
[10:22] Ravi: Cool — quick note: sometimes transcripts mislabel token boundary causing small reordering on very low-latency networks; it's rare but we have strategies. I'll show a brief log from an earlier run.
[10:33] (Ravi shares logs)
[10:36] Ravi: Here's a failure where the stream socket closed mid-generation — the client tried resume, there was a mismatch on the continuation token version because the model got swapped in the pool, we fell back to dedupe mode and returned a full regenerated completion. The takeaway: pin model family during critical flows.
[10:56] Aiko: Hmm, so if we want deterministic behavior we should both pin model and use canaries?
[11:01] Ravi: Correct. Pin the model version and perform canary rollouts with a small percent to validate changes.
[11:07] Kenji: For the POC bench you mentioned, what do you need from our side?
[11:11] Ravi: A small sample of ~500 representative prompts, token distribution, desired SLA numbers (p50/p95/p99), and a test account or sandbox to run in ap-northeast-1.
[11:19] Aiko: We'll assemble that and share by Tuesday.
[11:23] Maya: Fantastic. I'm going to show a short sequence of the SDK in Go implementing resume tokens and idempotency. (typing)
[11:34] [11:34] Maya: Code snippet: set X-Idempotency-Key, open event stream, on disconnect attempt resume with continuation token. If resume returns 404, send fresh request with same key.
[11:46] Dinesh: Do you provide client SDKs with that logic baked in?
[11:49] Maya: Our official SDKs for JS, Python have helpers. For Go we have a reference lib and a guide. We'll share links.
[11:59] Priya: One more on privacy — does Dedicated give us the option to disable analytics entirely?
[12:04] Sasha: Yes Dedicated + Private allow control plane options where we can disable telemetry collection or route telemetry to your endpoints. It's part of the enterprise package.
[12:15] Maya: Ok looks like we're approaching time — any final rapid-fire questions?
[12:20] Kenji: One: do you support model snapshots for rollbacks?
[12:23] Ravi: Yes model versions are immutable snapshots; you can revert to any prior version.
[12:27] Aiko: Two: are there examples of similar healthcare customers?
[12:30] Maya: We have non-identifiable case studies; I'll share redacted references.
[12:34] Priya: Three: timelines — we'd like a POC within 2-3 weeks. Is that feasible?
[12:39] Maya: Yes, if we get prompts and traffic by Tuesday we can spin a sandbox in ap-northeast-1 and run a two-week POC.
[12:45] (wrap-up)
[12:47] Maya: Recap and next steps: we'll share the sandbox invite, SOC2 + private deployment deck, the pricing worksheet, and Ravi will run a targeted latency run. Kenji will share traffic profile.
[12:59] Kenji: We'll do that. Thanks everyone.
[13:02] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links. Bye.
